video.title: The 100% REMOTE Boring Business That Almost Anyone Can Start

summary: Sergio explains a remote residential cleaning company that connects local customers with independent cleaners and earns a share of each job. The video describes how to choose a city, recruit and test cleaners, find customers, and convert first-time bookings into recurring cleans. Sergio presents Nate and Nate as a case study, claiming their business reached $60,000 a month in top-line revenue while they kept their furniture-store jobs. The main takeaway is that recurring demand and outsourced physical work can make a local service business easier to run remotely, though the results are promotional claims and the service still needs human quality control.

ideas.name: Remote residential cleaning company
ideas.one_liner: Own the local customer relationship and schedule, while independent cleaners perform residential cleaning.
ideas.business_model: Per-job service revenue, with the operator retaining a share of each clean; recurring weekly, bi-weekly, or monthly bookings.
ideas.customer: Households in a local city that need residential cleaning, including customers who want recurring service.
ideas.problem: Customers need their homes cleaned repeatedly. Independent cleaners may want steady jobs without doing their own marketing, sales, and customer conversations.
ideas.offer: Arrange and schedule home cleans through a local cleaning company; independent cleaners do the physical work and provide the in-home customer experience.

pricing.model: Per clean, with a stated operator share of each job and recurring customer bookings.
pricing.notes: Sergio also says roughly half goes to the cleaner and estimates a $150–$175 spread per job. He does not reconcile that estimate with the stated 50–60% operator share.

acquisition_channels.details: Post in local Facebook and Nextdoor groups. For the grand opening approach, post as a person rather than as a business, introduce yourself, mention the company, and offer neighbours a discount.

quote.text: You're going to post in local Facebook and Nextdoor groups, and basically something as simple as, "Hey, I'm looking for a reliable cleaner. Does anyone have any recommendations?"
quote.speaker: Sergio

acquisition_channels.details: Use a personal, relatable local post for the grand opening; Sergio suggests including family or a dog if available.
Sergio names Google LSA as a paid lead source.
Sergio names Thumbtack as a source of paid leads.
Run Meta ads, including Facebook and Instagram ads.
Set up a Google Business Profile as part of the local business foundation; the transcript does not specify an acquisition tactic using it.
For recruiting cleaners, ask local groups for recommendations; cleaners and neighbours may respond with referrals.

ideas.delivery: The operator connects customers to cleaners, schedules the work, and handles customer conversations and quality checks remotely. Independent cleaners travel to the home, clean it, and provide the in-home service. Sergio says cleaners should already have professional experience, transport, and equipment. If a clean is poor, the operator sends someone back to make it right.
unit_economics_claims: Sergio says a standard clean sells for USD 300–350 and estimates a USD 150–175 spread per job; see the linked metric claims.
Sergio says roughly 25% of customers convert to recurring cleans; this is a stated projection.
Sergio gives an illustrative scenario of two to three cleans per day and about USD 373 daily, USD 2,600 weekly, or USD 10,000 monthly; see the linked metric claims.

Sergio says Nate and Nate reached USD 10,000 monthly within a couple of months and later reported USD 60,000 monthly top-line revenue while working 15–20 combined hours per week; see the linked metric claims.
Profit, advertising cost per customer, cleaner utilization, refunds, and owner take-home are not stated.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated for the business as a whole. Sergio says a test clean costs USD 75–100; website, phone, and advertising costs are not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Sergio says Nate and Nate reached USD 10,000 per month within a couple of months, but does not say when their first revenue arrived.

acquisition.how: Paid ads and online listings can use software, but local positioning, posts, campaign decisions, and lead handling need human setup and routine review. Avoid unsolicited electronic outreach to individuals or sole traders in the UK.

onboarding.how: Cleaner sourcing, trust assessment, experience checks, and test cleans require human judgment and in-person work.

delivery.how: A cleaner must physically travel to and clean each home. Remote scheduling does not automate the physical service.

billing.how: Recurring payments could be handled with billing software, but the transcript names no payment system or automated billing process.

support.how: The operator makes a quality-control call after each job and must resolve complaints or arrange a return clean.

uk_applicability.notes: The local recurring-cleaning model transfers to the UK, but contractor status, tax, insurance, consumer rules, and local platform performance need UK-specific handling. The transcript's channels are mostly usable concepts, though local availability and costs may differ.

risks: Cleaner reliability and trust are the main operational challenge described; poor work can require a return visit and risk a bad review.
The cleaner must perform physical work in customers' homes, so the business is not fully unattended even if the owner operates remotely.
The stated gross spread does not include customer acquisition, payment processing, refunds, insurance, tax, or other operating costs.
The Nate and Nate example is top-line revenue; profit and owner take-home are not stated.
A UK operator should check whether the cleaners' working arrangements support independent-contractor status and arrange suitable contracts and insurance.
